KEY MESSAGE 1...Morning showers exit, followed by a brief lull this 
afternoon before a cold front brings additional showers and 
thunderstorms this evening. A few strong to isolated severe 
thunderstorms are possible.

As anticipated, gloomy conditions to wrap up the workweek. Earlier 
this morning, a warm front lifted through southern New England, 
bringing the first round of showers. The region is now positioned 
within the warm sector. Dew points are increasing into the lower 60s 
along the coast, while interior locations remain in the 50s. 
However, by midafternoon, anticipate temperatures and dew points 
continuing to climb into the 60s. Increasing dew points could lead 
to pockets of instability. High-resolution guidance suggests limited 
surface-based CAPE; however, as we've previously mentioned, the jet 
dynamics associated with the approaching cold front are impressive.

A line of showers and embedded thunderstorms is developing across 
western New York and extending southwest into Ohio. This activity is 
associated with our cold front, which is marching eastward, aided by 
a fairly robust mid-level trough. Ahead of the trough, SSW flow 
allows for WAA, supporting mild afternoon temperatures despite the 
clouds and rain. Highs should reach the middle 60s across northern 
areas, while upper 60s to near 70 degrees are possible farther south.

Today is not anticipated to be a high-end severe weather day by any 
stretch of the imagination; however, it is a day we cannot 
completely ignore. Instability remains limited, generally 100-300 
J/kg of MUCAPE, though strong bulk shear may compensate for the 
limited instability and support a few stronger storms. Over the last 
24 hours, the greatest shear has shifted a bit farther south, 
favoring areas around NYC and points southwest. Nevertheless, a 
couple of stronger storms remain possible. Feel as though these 
storms could produce sub-severe wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph, with a 
much lower chance of severe gusts exceeding 60 mph. CAMs continue to 
indicate that the greatest potential for thunderstorms across 
southern New England will be between 5 PM and 11 PM as the cold 
front progresses from west to east.

Additional rainfall amounts of 0.25 to 0.50 inches are expected.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A few showers may linger along the southern coast 
early Saturday. Otherwise, drier and noticeably colder conditions 
are expected Saturday.

Heading into the overnight hours, the area of low pressure 
associated with the cold front tracks northeast through the Saint 
Lawrence Valley as broad high pressure expands across the Great 
Plains. The surface low deepens to below 990 mb, with some guidance 
suggesting it could reach 985 mb by Saturday afternoon. A tightening 
pressure gradient supports gusty NNW winds at the surface, while 
northerly flow strengthens aloft. Meanwhile, 850 mb temperatures 
fall to between -6C and -4C, a rather significant drop considering 
values were between +15C and +17C Friday afternoon.

While the majority of precipitation should exit with the cold front, 
some guidance suggests the potential for an anafrontal wave to 
develop along the departing boundary early Saturday. This could 
allow showers to linger across the southern coast, Cape Cod, and the 
Islands into Saturday morning. Highs Saturday afternoon are not 
anticipated to be much warmer than the lower 50s across the coastal 
plain and middle to upper 40s farther inland. However, with gusty 
winds, apparent temperatures are expected to be 5 to 10 degrees 
colder than the actual air temperatures.

Very cold conditions are expected Saturday night into Sunday morning 
as strong high pressure builds into the region. With the combination 
of very cold temperatures aloft, diminishing winds, and favorable 
radiational cooling, temperatures are expected to fall below 
freezing across much of southern New England, leading to widespread 
frost/freeze conditions. However, since we are outside the 
climatological growing season, our frost/freeze program ended on 
October 11, and no Frost or Freeze headlines will be issued. 
Nevertheless, if you purchased any sensitive tropical plants or 
palms from the garden center this summer, now would be a good time 
to bring them indoors!

KEY MESSAGE 3...Dry with a modest warmup through mid next week, but 
monitoring coastal storminess near or south of the mid-Atlantic 
waters which could bring periods of light rain, enhanced northeast 
winds and building waves/possible erosion to southeast New England.

Expansive area of high pressure will maintain itself over most or 
much of Southern New England through midweek and potentially longer 
as it becomes reinforced by another strong high pressure coming out 
of the northern Canadian Prairie region by midweek. This will at
